title: 10 Family-Backed Investors, and When to Pitch Them
summary: 10 Family-Backed Investors, and When to Pitch Them
body_markdown:
A founder told to “talk to family offices” has been given a location, not a route. A family can invest straight into a startup, write a check to a fund, or do both through separate teams. To you, those are different investors. A team that picks fund managers may admire your company and still be unable to buy a share.


Start with the kind of capital you need. If you need someone to lead and price a round, ask that question early. If your lead is already in place, a team that joins alongside other investors could be an excellent fit. If you're building a business with a long development cycle, find out how the investor has handled a delay at another company. Having a long time horizon on a website doesn't tell you how they'll behave at a board meeting.


## Ten examples to research


These are public examples of family offices, their investment arms, or family-backed platforms. They aren't ranked and none is a claim that the investor is accepting pitches.


- [Peblinge Ventures](https://peblinge.com/) . Family office. Pre-seed/seed; B2B software appears in its stated focus. Could fit early B2B software; read actual portfolio before asking.
- [Mutschler Ventures](https://www.mutschler-ventures.com/) . Single-family-office venture arm. Early-stage; DACH connection is a useful filter. Look at its current sector exclusions and whether a lead is in place.
- [Smedvig Ventures](https://smedvigcapital.com/private-equity-funds/) . Smedvig family-office direct investment brand. Direct venture investing separate from family office fund allocations. Find a comparable direct deal and check geography and stage.
- [Raptor Group](https://www.raptorgroup.com/about) . Family-office-backed private investment firm. Publicly describes investing from early stage across several asset classes. Identify the relevant strategy and team before reaching out.
- [Bezos Expeditions](https://www.bezosexpeditions.com/) . Founder-backed investment vehicle. Provides a selected-investments list. Use past deals as evidence only; don't infer applications are open.
- [Emerson Collective](https://www.emersoncollective.com/our-work/venture-capital) . Founder-led organization with venture arm. Dedicated venture practice; review its published investment themes. Separate commercial venture fit from philanthropic activity.
- [Builders Vision](https://www.buildersvision.com/investments-partners/) . Family-backed investment and philanthropic platform. Public investment and partner page offers examples across its platforms. Confirm which team, mandate and program fits.
- [Aglaé Ventures](https://aglaeventures.com/philosophy) . Family-backed technology investor. Discloses technology investing from early opportunities through pre-IPO. Find an actual investment at your stage and in your market.
- [Klaris Capital](https://klariscapital.com/investments/) . Family-office-backed investment platform. Describes Series A to pre-IPO investments and selected co-investments. Check whether the relevant path is direct equity, co-investment or advisory.
- [Sobrato Family Holdings](https://www.sobrato.com/capital/portfolio/) . Pool within family capital platform. Discloses selective direct and co-investments in high-growth companies. Find evidence for a direct mandate rather than assuming a fund allocation can invest in your company.


## Before asking for an introduction


Find one directly comparable transaction and check the date. A search for the investor's name plus a comparable company often turns up a financing announcement. In your notes, separate who led from who participated. Then ask whether the team still backs companies that look like yours and which legal entity usually invests. A credible introduction is easier to make when you can explain both the match and the request in one sentence.


On the call, ask who makes the decision, how long diligence normally takes, and whether they keep capital available for future rounds. For a team that makes selective investments, ask what made the last one worth doing. If you're relying on the money to close on time, get the amount, decision owner and target date in writing. Don't plan payroll on the strength of a pleasant call.


The best outcome from the first conversation may be finding out that the fund allocator knows a direct investor. That's a useful answer. The mistake is spending three meetings trying to turn the wrong kind of capital into the right kind.
